metadata.title: Assessing AI in Educational Evaluation: A Comprehensive Analysis of ChatGPT’s Performance on PISA Reading Skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use student microdata from PISA; instead, it administers a fixed set of OECD-released PISA reading questions to ChatGPT and scores the model’s responses against OECD answer keys. Because there is no sampling of students, no complex survey design is involved and no PISA student/sampling weights can be applied. The analysis is therefore not a population-representative estimation of 15-year-olds’ reading literacy, but an evaluation of an AI system on selected items. The only “data preparation” step described is the selection of 45 released reading questions from 2000 and 45 from 2009, their categorization by text type/question type/difficulty/Bloom level, and scoring of correctness (including a second administration one week later for consistency).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variable is ChatGPT’s item-level correctness on OECD-provided PISA reading questions, not a PV-based cognitive achievement score for students. Missing-data handling is not reported because the dataset is generated from a controlled item-response procedure (ChatGPT answers to a fixed set of 90 questions) rather than from a student survey dataset with item nonresponse and PV estimation. As a result, there is no standard PV/missing-data pipeline to document in the way it would be required for PISA student achievement analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD-released PISA reading questions from the 2000 and 2009 assessments (45 questions from each year; 90 total). Questions were selected from the actual application items that were published/released for those years, and then categorized by PISA framework text type (continuous/non-continuous/multiple), question format (open-ended/multiple-choice/short answer/complex multiple-choice/closed structured), and OECD difficulty levels; additionally, 2000 and 2009 items were categorized by Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive domain. ChatGPT was asked the same set of questions twice within one week (second round one week later) using copy–paste; responses were scored using OECD answer keys (including partial/acceptable rules for open-ended items as described via the OECD question publication reports).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: ChatGPT reading item accuracy (correct vs incorrect)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Accuracy: 41/45 = 91% (Round 1); 41/45 = 91% (Round 2 reported overall as consistent with 91% baseline for 2000 items)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 Reading literacy released items the study evaluated ChatGPT’s item-level correctness (correct vs incorrect) across the selected reading questions, finding that ChatGPT achieved about 91% accuracy in both rounds. This indicates that large language models can reliably answer many PISA reading literacy items, suggesting potential for automating parts of reading assessment workflows, while still requiring careful item-type and difficulty-level checks before operational use.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Accuracy by PISA text type (continuous vs non-continuous)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across PISA text types, finding that accuracy was higher for continuous texts than for non-continuous texts. This indicates that policy and practice should treat text-format heterogeneity as a key constraint when using AI for reading assessment automation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Accuracy by question format (open-constructed, multiple-choice, short answer, complex multiple-choice, closed structured)
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2000: open-constructed 18/19 (94.7%); multiple-choice 19/21 (90.5%); short answer 1/1 (100%); complex multiple-choice 1/2 (50%); closed structured 2/2 (100%)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 Reading literacy released items the study evaluated ChatGPT’s correctness across question formats, finding that accuracy was very high for open-constructed and closed/short-answer formats but substantially lower for complex multiple-choice items. This indicates that AI-assisted assessment may work well for simpler response structures while complex multi-part items require human review or improved AI prompting/vision support.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across OECD difficulty levels, finding that accuracy was perfect at some lower levels but declined at higher difficulty (notably Level 2 and Level 5). This indicates that AI-based assessment support may be more reliable for easier items and should be constrained or supplemented for higher-difficulty reading tasks.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Accuracy by Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive domain
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2000: Remember 7/8 (87.5%); Understand 18/20 (90%); Application 7/7 (100%); Analysis 5/5 (100%); Assessment 4/5 (80%); Creation 0/0 (no items)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive domains, finding that performance was weakest for the Assessment domain. This indicates that AI may be less dependable for higher-order evaluative reading tasks, so educators should be cautious when using AI to support assessment of evaluation-level competencies.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: ChatGPT reading item accuracy (correct vs incorrect)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Accuracy: 41/45 = 91% (overall reported as 91% in both rounds); by text type: continuous 95.7% (22/23), non-continuous 80.0% (12/15), multiple 100% (7/7)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading literacy released items the study evaluated ChatGPT’s item-level correctness (correct vs incorrect) across the selected reading questions, finding that ChatGPT achieved about 91% accuracy overall while showing lower performance on non-continuous texts. This indicates that integrating ChatGPT into assessment processes may be feasible for continuous-text reading items but may require additional safeguards or alternative handling for non-continuous/visual formats.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Accuracy by PISA text type (continuous vs non-continuous vs multiple)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across PISA text types, finding that performance was highest for multiple-text items and lowest for non-continuous texts. This indicates that educational evaluation systems using AI should prioritize continuous/mixed textual items first and implement additional procedures for non-continuous (graph/map/image-based) items.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Accuracy by question format (open-constructed, multiple-choice, short answer, complex multiple-choice, closed structured)
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2009: open-constructed 12/13 (92.3%); multiple-choice 22/24 (91.7%); short answer 4/5 (80%); complex multiple-choice 1/1 (100%); closed constructed response 2/2 (100%)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading literacy released items the study evaluated ChatGPT’s correctness across question formats, finding that accuracy remained above 90% for open-constructed and multiple-choice items but dropped for short-answer items. This indicates that when deploying AI for reading assessment, item-format-specific calibration (e.g., stricter scoring rules or additional verification for short answers) is important.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across OECD difficulty levels, finding that accuracy dropped most strongly at Level 5 while remaining perfect at several other levels. This indicates that AI integration into assessment should include difficulty-aware routing (e.g., human verification for Level 5 items).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Accuracy by Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive domain
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2009: Remember 10/11 (90.9%); Understand 17/18 (94.4%); Application 2/2 (100%); Analysis 5/7 (71.4%); Assessment 7/7 (100%); Creation 0/0 (no items)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across Bloom’s taxonomy cognitive domains, finding that accuracy was lowest for the Analysis domain. This indicates that AI-assisted assessment may require additional checks for analytical reading processes, even when overall accuracy is high.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 & 2009 Reading literacy (released items; item-level scoring across two administrations)
main_findings.target_variable: Consistency of ChatGPT answers over time (Round 1 vs Round 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2000: Round 1 41 correct/4 incorrect; Round 2 corrected 3 previously incorrect but still had 1 incorrect in both rounds (overall incorrect count changed from 4 to 1 for the persistent error pattern). 2009: Round 1 41 correct/4 incorrect; Round 2 40 correct/5 incorrect; corrected 2 previously incorrect but still had 2 incorrect in both rounds.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 and 2009 Reading literacy released items the study compared ChatGPT’s correctness across two administrations one week apart, finding that ChatGPT sometimes corrected earlier mistakes but also produced new errors and inconsistent answers for some items. This indicates that any educational integration should treat AI scoring as non-deterministic and should incorporate re-checking or ensemble/verification strategies rather than assuming stable item-level correctness.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates ChatGPT’s ability to answer PISA reading literacy questions by administering 90 OECD-released items (45 from PISA 2000 and 45 from PISA 2009) to ChatGPT twice within one week and scoring responses against OECD answer keys. Across both rounds, ChatGPT achieved an overall accuracy of about 91% for the selected PISA reading items. Performance varied systematically by item characteristics: accuracy was higher for continuous texts than non-continuous texts (e.g., in 2000: 93.9% vs 83.3%; in 2009: 95.7% vs 80.0%), and complex multiple-choice items showed the lowest success in 2000 (50%). Accuracy also depended on difficulty and Bloom’s taxonomy, with weaker results at higher difficulty levels and in analytical/evaluative domains. The study is not a student-based PISA analysis (no PVs, no survey weights) and does not train ML models; therefore, results reflect AI item-response behavior rather than population achievement, and inconsistency across rounds limits reliability for high-stakes assessment.
